newsitem.title: USA: U.S. election results show pro-civility landslide.
newsitem.headline: U.S. election results show pro-civility landslide.

text.p: Without mentioning President Bill Clinton, Bob Dole or Newt Gingrich, the queen of American etiquette known as "Miss Manners" indicted them all on Tuesday as she hailed U.S. elections as a pro-civility landslide.

"We had a national referendum on whether we want a civil society and it wasn't really much of a cliff-hanger," Miss Manners, also known as Judith Martin, told a terribly polite audience. "... The American romance with rudeness is over."
Noting that every candidate at every level of government campaigned for a more civil society, Martin noted that there was little agreement on what that meant.

"Politicians, I notice, were defining it as a requirement that their opponents stop bringing up embarrassing information about them," she said. "And the voters this year came up with the concept of negativism, which came to mean that it's rude to disagree with anyone or criticise anyone, which makes it a little bit difficult to air the issues or make a case for voting for one person over another."

Speaking to a mostly female, largely senior luncheon group at the Woman's National Democratic Club, Martin said the civility trend surfaced after decades of do-one's-own-thing, meanness-equals-power freedom, which simply did not work.
"In politics they used to say that nice guys finish last," she said. "Well, only if the public votes to have the rude people finish first, which is what happened as recently as two years ago."

Martin, who writes a nationally syndicated column on etiquette and has published several books on the subject, made no specific reference to congressional Republicans who came to power in 1994, but the audience nodded knowingly. Hatted heads bobbed; sensible shoes were crossed at the ankle.
The tide turned toward manners after the federal government shutdown last year, Martin said.

"The public did not, as expected, say 'Look at all these wonderfully idealistic people who refuse to compromise.' They said, 'These are a bunch of nasty egomaniacs showing off and they don't care about us.'"

The nub of the problem, she said, was the propensity to make law take care of situations where etiquette might have done the job. As examples, she mentioned recent trends to legislate responses to tobacco smoking and sexual harassment.

"When we enlarge the scope of law to enforce manners it really does threaten our freedom ... People should have a legal right to be obnoxious," Martin said, adding that the offenders must be prepared to take the consequences.
People who fail to respond to invitations came in for criticism, as did aggressive drivers and non-smokers who offer insults in the guise of "health advice" to smokers.
After the speech, in response to questions, she singled out President Bill Clinton for praise, but not for any of his actions as the head of state.
He got kudos for gracefully accepting the televised apology of veteran newsman David Brinkley, after Brinkley called him a "bore" in an election-night broadcast.
"It is extremely gracious to forgive, to do with a built-in excuse and the most gracious of all excuses is, 'Oh I might have done that myself.' So I thought the president did very well on that."
